HuYgTa-d1e91.summary: Prologue to Book 1 of Thomas of Strasbourg's commentary on the Sentences. It opens with an inaugural sermon on 'Dedit abyssus vocem suam' (Hab 3:10), which commends Scripture as God's voice, the graced medium of beatitude in this life, by its four causes, and commends the four books of the Sentences. Three further 'circa textum' sections divide the Lombard's prologue according to its rhetorical aim of making readers benevolent, attentive and docile. Each introduces one of four questions that together form Thomas's account of theology. Q.1 holds that God is the subject of the wayfarer's theology not under the infinite, absolute ratio of deity but under a special ratio: supremely lovable truth proportioned to a soul not yet in glory, in agreement with Giles of Rome's 'Deus ut glorificator'. Q.2 holds that this theology is truly a science according to the knower's capacity, with the articles of faith as its principles. It is subalternate only broadly to the science of God and the blessed, it is properly wisdom, and it is one science because its object is one. Q.3 argues that by absolute power God could give a wayfarer intuitive vision without ending his state as wayfarer, since beatitude consists in fruition. It denies, against Scotus, that perfect abstractive knowledge of the divine essence is possible, and it holds that faith can coexist with vision, science and opinion. Q.4 concludes that since a science is named from its end, and theology's end is the love of God, theology is properly 'affective', a third genus beyond the speculative and the practical. A single thesis unifies the prologue: theology is defined by its end, the love of God, and both its subject (Q.1) and its genus (Q.4) are specified by that end.
claims: Scripture, as God's voice, is the medium by which the soul is joined to God in this life.
God is the subject of the wayfarer's theology under a special, finite ratio named from theology's end, not under the infinite ratio of deity.
The wayfarer's theology is truly a science, with the articles of faith as principles, though only according to the capacity of the knower.
Theology is broadly, not properly, subalternate to the science of God and the blessed, and is properly wisdom.
By absolute power God can grant a wayfarer intuitive vision of the divine essence; perfect abstractive knowledge of it is impossible.
Faith can coexist with clear vision, science and opinion.
A science is named from its end; the end of theology is the love of God, so theology is properly affective, neither speculative nor practical.
The Lombard's prologue is ordered to render readers benevolent, attentive and docile.

HuYgTa-d1e2771.summary: Book 1, Distinction 37, on the presence of God in things and the location of spiritual substances. The 'circa textum' divides the Lombard's text into true modes of divine presence (by grace in some things, by nature in all things, and by essence without circumscription or determination of place) and false modes, which the Lombard rejects. The single question, 'An substantia quaelibet spiritualis loco existat', takes up God, the angel, the rational soul and universal nature in turn. God alone has proper, simple ubiquity: he is present everywhere attingently and conservatively, but neither circumscriptively nor definitively. Angels and souls are in place definitively, never circumscriptively. They are located by the operative application of their power, not by bare essence, are confined by natural power to one place at a time, and move locally in time rather than in an instant. Universal nature is in place and moves only derivatively, through its particulars. Boethius's dictum that incorporeal things are not in place is reconciled by restricting it to circumscriptive location.
claims: God is present in things by grace, by nature and by essence, without circumscription or determination of place.
God alone possesses per se, simple ubiquity: attingent and conservative presence everywhere, neither circumscriptive nor definitive.
Angels and rational souls are definitively, not circumscriptively, in place through the operative application of their power.
A created spirit is confined by natural power to one place at a time and moves locally in time.
Universal nature is in place and in motion only derivatively, through the particulars in which it exists.
Boethius's denial that incorporeals are in place applies only to circumscriptive location.

HuYgTa-d1e5268.summary: Book 2, Distinctions 43 and 44, the final distinctions of the book. The 'circa textum' follows the Lombard's move from sin in general to the gravest sin, the sin against the Holy Spirit, and its irremissibility, and then to the origin of the power to sin and of the power to dominate. The single question, 'An peccatum aliquod sit simpliciter irremissibile', is resolved in four articles. (1) There is a sin against the Holy Spirit, analyzed into four proper species on a physician/medicine/patient/sickness scheme. (2) It is irremissible only in that it lacks any excusing circumstance and leads to impenitence, never as exceeding God's power. (3) Every power to sin is from God, both its positive principle and its defectibility, which God causes negatively by withdrawing his sustaining influence. Sin's deformity, however, comes from the evil will. (4) Every power to dominate is from God, both in itself and in its licit acquisition and use. Christians owe obedience to an infidel ruler whose rule is just, but not to one whose rule is unjustly acquired or abusively exercised.
claims: No sin is irremissible with respect to God's power; sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible because it contains no excusing circumstance.
There are properly four species of sin against the Holy Spirit.
The power to sin, including its defectibility, is from God, while sin's moral deformity is from the evil will.
Dominion as such and its just exercise are from God.
Obedience is owed to a justly ruling infidel prince, but not to one whose rule is unjustly acquired or abused.

HuYgTa-d1e6333.summary: Book 3, Distinction 23, where the Lombard begins his treatment of the virtues of Christ and his members with faith considered absolutely: its definition and its object, things not apparent. Thomas's question asks whether faith is a virtue, and he answers through a general theory of habit. A habit is principally an absolute quality that connotes a relation to its object. It is neither a relation, nor a compound of absolute and relation, nor a mere mode. Habits are innate only in aptitude and acquired through exercise. The first moral virtue needs many acts to overcome contrary dispositions from original sin and custom, whereas a speculative habit can come from a single demonstration. We need habits to act well, not to act at all, and habit and power together cause the whole modified act. Applying this, acquired faith can be vicious. Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a praiseworthy habit ordered to meritorious assent, but not in Aristotle's strict sense of a power's ultimate perfection, which belongs to the light of glory. The habit of faith is compatible with clear vision.
claims: A habit is principally an absolute quality that connotes a relation, not a relation or a mere mode.
The first moral virtue cannot be acquired by one act, but a speculative habit can.
Habits are needed for acting well and cause the modified act together with the power.
Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense but not in the strict Aristotelian sense.
Acquired faith can be a vicious habit.

HuYgTa-d1e6400.summary: Book 3, Distinctions 24 and 25, treated together, where the Lombard considers faith comparatively: with respect to its object, as concerning things unseen, and with respect to believers, as required for salvation in every age. Thomas's question asks whether falsehood can underlie faith. Properly speaking, the object of faith is God alone, the first truth; broadly, it is the articles and what is annexed to them. No falsehood can underlie infused faith, formed or unformed, because it comes from uncreated truth, rests on infallible divine authority, and concerns contingent truths only as ordained by God, that is, under his ordained rather than absolute power. Acquired faith can be false. Apparent counterexamples from prophecy, the timing of the Incarnation, adoration of an unconsecrated host and Abraham's faith are resolved through distinctions such as conditional prophecy and conditional latria. There are twelve articles, after the Apostles' Creed; demonstrable truths such as God's unity are excluded. Following Hugh of St Victor, Thomas holds that before the Gospel only a minimum of explicit faith, in God as creator and redeemer, was required. The faith of all ages is one but differs in explicitness.
claims: God alone is the principal object of faith.
No falsehood can underlie infused faith; acquired faith can be false.
Faith concerns contingent truths as falling under God's ordained power.
There are twelve articles of faith, and demonstrable truths are not articles.
Before the Gospel, only a minimum of explicit faith in God as creator and redeemer was required for salvation.

HuYgTa-d1e86.summary: Book 1 of Thomas of Strasbourg's commentary on the Sentences. This summary is PARTIAL: it rests only on the Prologue and Distinction 37, 2 of the book's 43 divisions. The Prologue gives Thomas's account of theology. God is its subject under a special ratio, supremely lovable truth proportioned to the wayfarer, rather than under the infinite ratio of deity. Theology is a true science according to the capacity of the knower, with the articles of faith as principles, and it is properly wisdom. By absolute power a wayfarer could receive intuitive vision, and faith can coexist with vision and science. Because theology is named from its end, the love of God, it is 'affective', neither speculative nor practical. Distinction 37 treats the presence of God and of spirits in place. God alone has simple ubiquity, attingent and conservative, neither circumscriptive nor definitive. Angels and souls are in place definitively, through the operative application of their power, are confined to one place at a time, and move in time. Universal nature is located only through its particulars. The intervening distinctions on the Trinity, the divine attributes and other topics are not covered here.
claims: God is the subject of the wayfarer's theology under a special ratio named from its end, the love of God.
The wayfarer's theology is a true science, with the articles of faith as principles, and is properly wisdom.
Theology is properly affective, a genus beyond the speculative and the practical.
God alone possesses simple ubiquity, present everywhere neither circumscriptively nor definitively.
Created spirits are definitively in place through the operative application of their power.

HuYgTa-d1e3238.summary: Book 2 of Thomas of Strasbourg's commentary on the Sentences. This summary is PARTIAL: it rests only on Distinctions 43-44, the final division of the book, 1 of its 34 direct children. Its prologue and the distinctions on creation, angels, human nature, grace and sin are not covered. In the covered material Thomas asks whether any sin is simply irremissible. He holds that the sin against the Holy Spirit, which has four proper species, is irremissible only because it lacks any excusing circumstance and induces impenitence, never because it exceeds God's power. The power to sin and its defectibility come from God, though sin's deformity comes from the evil will. Dominion and its just use are likewise from God, and Christians owe obedience to a just infidel ruler but not to an unjust or abusive one.
claims: No sin is irremissible with respect to God's power.
Sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible because it lacks any excusing circumstance.
The power to sin and its defectibility are from God; sin's deformity is from the evil will.
Dominion and its just exercise are from God, and obedience is owed to a just infidel ruler.

HuYgTa-d1e5329.summary: Book 3 of Thomas of Strasbourg's commentary on the Sentences. This summary is PARTIAL: it rests only on Distinctions 23 and 24-25, 2 of the book's 28 direct divisions. The Prologue and the distinctions on the Incarnation, Christ's knowledge and merit, redemption, hope, charity, the cardinal virtues, the gifts and the commandments are not covered. The covered material opens the treatise on the virtues with faith. In Distinction 23 Thomas develops a general theory of habit: an absolute quality connoting a relation, acquired by exercise, needed for acting well, and causing the modified act together with the power. He concludes that infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense of a praiseworthy, meritorious habit, though not in Aristotle's strict sense, since the light of glory surpasses it. In Distinctions 24-25 he holds that God is the principal object of faith and that no falsehood can underlie infused faith, because it rests on divine authority and concerns contingents as ordained by God. He counts twelve articles following the Apostles' Creed, and he holds that before the Gospel a minimum of explicit faith in God as creator and redeemer sufficed for salvation.
claims: A habit is principally an absolute quality connoting a relation, acquired by exercise and necessary for acting well.
Infused faith is a virtue in the broad sense but not in the strict Aristotelian sense.
No falsehood can underlie infused faith, whose principal object is God.
Before the Gospel, only a minimum of explicit faith was necessary for salvation.

HuYgTa.summary: Thomas of Strasbourg's commentary on the four books of Peter Lombard's Sentences. This summary is PARTIAL and rests on only a small fraction of the work: from Book 1, the Prologue and Distinction 37; from Book 2, Distinctions 43-44; from Book 3, Distinctions 23 and 24-25. Book 4 has no interpretations yet. In the Prologue Thomas defines theology by its end, the love of God. God is its subject under a special ratio proportioned to the wayfarer. Theology is a true science and wisdom, with the articles of faith as its principles, and it is properly 'affective', neither speculative nor practical. Book 1, Distinction 37 holds that God alone is simply ubiquitous and that created spirits are definitively in place through the application of their power. Book 2, Distinctions 43-44 hold that no sin exceeds God's power to forgive: sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible only for want of excuse. Both the power to sin and the power to dominate come from God, and obedience to infidel rulers depends on the justice of their rule. Book 3, Distinctions 23-25 ground the treatment of faith in a theory of habit as an absolute quality connoting a relation. Infused faith is a virtue in a broad but not a strict sense; God is its principal object; and no falsehood can underlie it. There are twelve articles, and before the Gospel a minimum of explicit faith sufficed. Other recurring features of the covered material are a careful use of the distinction between God's absolute and ordained power and dialogue with Giles of Rome, Scotus and Henry of Ghent.
claims: Theology is defined by its end, the love of God, and is properly affective.
The wayfarer's theology is a true science according to the capacity of the knower, with the articles of faith as principles.
God alone possesses simple ubiquity; created spirits are definitively in place through their operative power.
No sin is irremissible with respect to God's power.
Infused faith is an infallible virtue, in a broad sense, whose principal object is God.
